label: Z(X)=B(X)
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Z(X)=B(X)}
If $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ is a reduced measurable space, then  $(X, \tau_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}})$ is a $P$-space.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $Z=Z(f)$ for some $f\in C(X)$ and $p\in Z$. Since $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$ is a base for the open sets, for every $n\ge1$, there exists a measurable set $A_n\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}$ such that $p\in A_n\subseteq f^{-1}(-\frac{1}{n}, \frac{1}{n})$. Hence $A_0=\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty A_n\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}$ and $p\in A_0\subseteq Z$. This shows that $Z$ is open (clopen) and then by \cite[4J]{GJ}, we conclude that $(X, \tau_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}})$ is a $P$-space.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md: Let $X=\mathbb R$ be the set of all real numbers and $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$ be the  algebra generated by the family $\{[a, b) : a, b\in \mathbb R \text{ and } a<b \}$. Now, clearly $\tau_{\mathbb R}\subseteq \tau_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}$, where $\tau_{\mathbb R}$ is the usual topology on $\mathbb R$. Therefore, the identity function $i : (X, \tau_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}})\to \mathbb R$ is continuous, but $Z(f)=\{0\}$ is not a clopen subset of $ (X, \tau_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}})$.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md: Let $\mathfrak M$ be the $\sigma$-algebra of Lebesgue measurable sets of $\mathbb R^n$. Then it is easy to see that $\mathfrak M|_{\mathbb R^m}$ is the $\sigma$-algebra of Lebesgue measurable sets of $\mathbb R^m$, for any $1\le m<n$.

body_md: Since $(T, \operatorname{\mathcal A}')$ is an  extension of $X$,  $ A'\cap X\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}$, for any $ A'\in \operatorname{\mathcal A}'$. On the other hand, for any $A\in \operatorname{\mathcal A}$ there is an elementary set $ A'\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}'$ such that $A= A'\cap X$ and thus $\text{cl}_T A=\text{cl}_T ( A'\cap X)= A'$, as $X$ is dense in $T$ and $ A'$ is clopen in $(T, \tau_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}'})$.

body_md: Let $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ and $(Y, \operatorname{\mathcal A}')$ are two elementary spaces. title: Definition
body_md: Let $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ be an elementary space, $Y$ a topological space and $f : X\to Y$ a mapping. Then $f$ is called $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-measurable if $f^{-1}(V)\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}$, for every open subset $V\subseteq Y$.

label: units
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{units}
Let $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ be an elementary space. Then an element $f\in M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ is unit if and only if $Z(f)=\emptyset$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Necessity. Suppose that $f\in M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ is unit, then $fg=1$, for some $g\in M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$. This implies that $Z(f)\subseteq Z(fg)=Z(1)=\emptyset$.

Sufficiency. If $Z(f)=\emptyset$, then $g=\frac{1}{f}=h\circ f$, where $h(x)=\frac{1}{x}\in C(\mathbb R)$. Now, since  a continuous function of an $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-measurable function is  $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-measurable and $fg=1$, we are done.

label: A-ultrafilters on X
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{A-ultrafilters on X}
Let $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$  be an elementary subspace of   an elementary space  $(T, \operatorname{\mathcal A}')$,  $A_0\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}$ and $p\in\text{cl}_TA_0$. Then there is at least one $\mathcal A$-ultrafilter on $X$ that contains $A_0$ and convergence to $p$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal F:=\{ A'\cap X :  A'\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}' \text{ and } p\in  A'\}$. Since $p\in\text{cl}_TA_0$,  Lemma \ref{m-sets of extensions} implies that $A_0\in\mathcal F$. On the other hand,  $p\in\text{cl}_TX$ follows   that $\mathcal F$ is an $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-filter on $X$ and so it's enough to show that it is an $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-ultrafilter, as clearly $\mathcal F$ is convergent to $p$. To let this end, suppose that $A\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}$, thus there exists an elementary set $ A'\in \operatorname{\mathcal A}'$ such that $A= A'\cap X$, as  $X$ is an elementary subspace of   $T$. On the other hand,
$$p\in\text{cl}_TX=\text{cl}_T(A\cup (X\setminus A))=\text{cl}_TA\cup\text{cl}_T(X\setminus A),$$
  implies that $p\in \text{cl}_TA$ or $p\in\text{cl}_T(X\setminus A)$. If $p\in\text{cl}_TA$,  Then
$$p\in \text{cl}_TA=\text{cl}_T( A'\cap X)\subseteq A',$$
which it follows  that $A\in\mathcal F$. The other case implies that $X\setminus A\in\mathcal F$. This  shows that $\mathcal F$ is an $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-ultrafilter by Lemma \ref{A-ultrafilter}(2).

label: Extensions
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{Extensions}
If  $(T, \operatorname{\mathcal A}')$ is an  extension of an elementary space $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$, then every point of $T$ is the limit of a unique  $\mathcal A$-ultrafilter 
$$\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p=\{ A'\cap X :  A'\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}' \text{ and } p\in  A' \}=\{A\in \operatorname{\mathcal A} : p\in\text{cl}_TA\}, $$
 on $X$. Moreover, if $\operatorname{\mathcal A}'$  is a $\sigma$-algebra, then  $\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$ is closed under countable intersection.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Since $X$ is  dense in $T$,  every point of $T$ is the limit of at least one $\mathcal A$-ultrafilter on $X$, by Lemma \ref{A-ultrafilters on X}. On the other hand, using Lemma \ref{A-ultrafilter}(3), distinct $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-ultrafilters on $X$ contains disjoint members of $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$. Thus, distinct $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-ultrafilters on $X$ can not have a common limit point in $T$.  The last statement is evident.

label: m-homo extension
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{m-homo extension}
Let $(T, \operatorname{\mathcal A}')$ be an  extension of an elementary space $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$. Then every elementary homomorphism $\varphi $ from $X$ into any reduced compact elementary space  $(Y, \tilde\operatorname{\mathcal A})$  extends to an elementary homomorphism  $\bar \varphi $ on $T$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, to define $\bar\varphi$ on $T$, let $p\in T$ and $\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$ be the unique $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-ultrafilter on $X$ converges to $p$, which obtained by Corollary \ref{Extensions}. Define 
$$\varphi^{\#}\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p=\{\tilde A\in \tilde\operatorname{\mathcal A} : \varphi^{-1}(\tilde A)\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p \}.$$
It is clear that $\varphi^{\#}\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$ is an $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-ultrafilter (on $Y$)  by Lemma \ref{A-ultrafilter}(2). Now, using Lemma \ref{T-compactness}, $\bigcap \varphi^{\#}\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$ is a singleton. Let $\bar\varphi(p)$ be this single point, i.e., $\bigcap \varphi^{\#}\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p=\{\bar\varphi(p)\}$.

Next, to see that $\bar\varphi$ is an extension of $\varphi$, note that for any $x\in X$,
$$\varphi^{\#}\operatorname{\mathcal A}_x=\{\tilde A\in \tilde\operatorname{\mathcal A} : \varphi^{-1}(\tilde A)\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}_x\}=\{\tilde A\in \tilde\operatorname{\mathcal A} : \varphi(x)\in \tilde A\}=:\tilde\operatorname{\mathcal A}_{\varphi(x)}.$$
Clearly, $\bigcap\tilde\operatorname{\mathcal A}_{\varphi(x)}=\{\varphi(x)\}$, which means $\bar\varphi(x)=\varphi(x)$.

Finally, we show that $\bar\varphi$ is an elementary homomorphism. Using the definition of $\bar\varphi$, for any $\tilde A\in \tilde\operatorname{\mathcal A}$ we have 
$$\bar\varphi^{-1}(\tilde A)=\{ p\in T : \bar\varphi(p)\in \tilde A \}=\{ p\in T : \varphi^{-1}(\tilde A)\in \operatorname{\mathcal A}^p \}=\text{cl}_T\varphi^{-1}(\tilde A),$$
 by  Corollary \ref{Extensions}. Also, the last term belongs to $ \operatorname{\mathcal A}'$, by Lemma \ref{m-sets of extensions},  which means that $\bar\varphi$ is an elementary homomorphism.
head: environment

label: Extension into compact
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Extension into compact}
Let  $(T, \operatorname{\mathcal A}')$  be an  extension of an elementary space $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$. Then every $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-measurable mapping $\varphi$ from $X$ into any  compact topological space $Y$, extends to a continuous mapping $\bar \varphi$ on $(T, \tau_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}'})$. Moreover, if $\operatorname{\mathcal A}'$ is a $\sigma$-algebra and $Y$ is second countable, then the extended mapping $\bar\varphi$  is $\operatorname{\mathcal A}'$-measurable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, to define $\bar\varphi$ on $T$, let $p\in T$ and $\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$ be the unique $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-ultrafilter on $X$ converges to $p$, which obtained by Corollary \ref{Extensions}. Define
$$\varphi^{\#}\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p=\{ Z\in Z(Y) : \varphi^{-1}(Z)\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p \}.$$
Note that, since $\varphi$ is $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-measurable, $\varphi^{-1}(Z)\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}$, for any $Z\in Z(Y)$.
It is easy to see that $\varphi^{\#}\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$  is a prime $z$-filter on $Y$. It follows then, $\varphi^{\#}\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$ has a limit point in $Y$, by \cite[Theorems 3.17 and 4.11]{GJ}. Take this limit point as $\bar\varphi(p)$, i.e., 
$$\bigcap \varphi^{\#}\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p=\{\bar\varphi(p)\}.$$
This defines a mapping $\bar \varphi$ from $T$ into $Y$. Whenever $p\in X$ then, $Z\in \varphi^{\#}\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$  if and only if $p\in \varphi^{-1}(Z)$ or equivalently $\varphi(p)\in Z$ and this implies that $\varphi(p)\in\bigcap \varphi^{\#}\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$, i.e., $\bar\varphi(p)=\varphi(p)$. This shows that $\bar \varphi$ is an extension of $\varphi$.

 Next, to show that $\bar\varphi$ is continuous at $p\in T$, suppose that $ U$ is a neighborhood of $\bar\varphi(p)$ in $Y$. Since $Y$ is completely regular, there are  zero-sets $\tilde Z_0, \tilde Z_1\in Z(Y)$  such that $\bar\varphi(p)\in Y\setminus \tilde Z_1 \subseteq\tilde Z_0\subseteq U$, see \cite[Theorem 3.2 and 3.2(b)]{GJ}. This  implies that $\tilde Z_1\notin \varphi^{\#}\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$, and since $\varphi^{\#}\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$ is prime and $\tilde Z_0 \cup\tilde Z_1=Y$, we conclude that $\tilde Z_0\in\varphi^{\#}\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$. Therefore $\varphi^{-1}(\tilde Z_0)\in \operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$ and since $X$ is an elementary subspace of $(T, \operatorname{\mathcal A}')$, we may choose an elementary set  $A'_0\in \operatorname{\mathcal A}'$ such that $\varphi^{-1}(\tilde Z_0)=A'_0\cap X$. To complete the proof, it is enough to show that $\bar\varphi(A'_0)\subseteq U$,  as $A'_0$ is a neighborhood of $p$. Let $q\in A'_0$. Thus $A'_0\cap X\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}^q$, by Corollary \ref{Extensions}, and hence $\tilde Z_0 \in\varphi^{\#}\operatorname{\mathcal A}^q$. It follows then $\bar\varphi(q)\in \tilde Z_0\subseteq U$ and we are done.

Finally,  for the last part of the theorem,  suppose that  $\operatorname{\mathcal A}'$ is a $\sigma$-algebra and  $Y$ is second countable, then $Y$  is metrizable by \cite[Theorem 4.2.8]{E}. Thus, every open subset $U\subseteq Y$ is a countable union of open balls, as $Y$ is second countable; see also \cite[Theorem 1.1.15]{E}. Using this, it is enough to show that $\bar\varphi^{-1}(B(y, r))\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}'$, for any  open ball $B(y, r)$. If $U=B(y_0, r_0)$ is an open ball  with center at some point $y_0\in Y$ and radius $r_0$, we may write
$$U=\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}B(y_0, r_n)=\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}\overline{B(y_0, r_n)},$$
where $r_n$ is an ascending sequence of positive real numbers converges to $r_0$ and in here  $\overline{B(y_0, r_n)}$ is the closure of $B(y_0, r_n)$ in $Y$. Now, since $\varphi$ is  $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-measurable and $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ is an elementary subspace of $(T, \operatorname{\mathcal A}')$, there is a measurable set $A'_n\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}'$ such that $\varphi^{-1}(B(y_0, r_n))=A'_n\cap X$, for every $n\ge1$. Using the continuty of $\bar\varphi$, it follows that
$$\bar\varphi(A'_n)=\bar\varphi(\text{cl}_T(A'_n\cap X))\subseteq\text{cl}_Y\varphi(A'_n\cap X)\subseteq\overline{B(y_0, r_n)}.$$
 Therefore $A'_0=\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}A'_n\subseteq\bar\varphi^{-1}(U)$ and $A'_0\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}'$. For the reverse inclusion, note that 
$$\varphi^{-1}(U)=\varphi^{-1}(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}{B(y_0, r_n)})=\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}A'_n\cap X=A'_0\cap X,$$
 which implies that $\varphi(X\setminus A'_0)\subseteq Y\setminus U$. Since $\text{cl}_T(X\setminus A'_0)=T\setminus A'_0$, so  by  the  continuty of $\bar\varphi$ we conclude that $\bar\varphi(T\setminus A'_0)\subseteq Y\setminus U$ which means $\bar\varphi^{-1}(U)\subseteq A'_0$, and the proof is complete.

label: beta X
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\begin{enumerate}
\item This is due to Theorem \ref{m-homo extension}.
\item This is a consequence of Theorem \ref{Extension into compact}.
\item We define an elementary homomorphism $\varphi : (T, \operatorname{\mathcal A}')\to (\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X, \bar\operatorname{\mathcal A})$ which is an isomorphism between $(T, \operatorname{\mathcal A}')$  and $(\varphi(T), \bar\operatorname{\mathcal A}|_{\varphi(T)})$. Let $p\in T$ and 
$$\mathcal F^p=\{ A'\cap X :  A'\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}' \text{ and } p\in  A' \}, $$ 
be the unique $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-ultrafilter obtained by Corollary \ref{Extensions}. Using  the argument before this result, $\mathcal F^p$ has  a unique convergent point in $\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$ and we let   $\varphi(p)$ to be this unique point.
 Using Corollary \ref{Extensions}, the mapping $\varphi$ just defined, is a monomorphism from $T$ into $\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$. Now, if $A'\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}'$, then $A'\cap X=A\in \operatorname{\mathcal A}$ and  by  the argument preceding the corollary, $\bar{A}=\text{cl}_{\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X}A=\{q\in\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X : A\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}^q\}$. Thus, another application of Corollary \ref{Extensions}, implies that $p\in A'$ if and only if $A\in\mathcal F^p$ and this is equivalent to saying that $\varphi(p)\in \text{cl}_{\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X}A$, i.e.
$\varphi(A')= \bar{A}\cap \varphi(T)$. Hence $T$ and $\varphi(T)$ are elementary isomorphic and hence
$(\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X, \bar\operatorname{\mathcal A})$ is an  extension of $T$.
\item Since $\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}'}T$ is an  elementary extension of $T$ (and hence  an  extension of $X$), and $\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$ is an extension of $T$, the result follows from (3). 
\item Using the argument preceding the corollary, $p\in \text{cl}_{\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X} A\cap \text{cl}_{\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X} B$ implies that $A , B\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$. Now, since $\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$ is a $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-filter, we conclude that $A\cap B\in \operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$, i.e., $p\in\text{cl}_{\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X}(A\cap B)$.
\end{enumerate}

label: G-K theorem
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{G-K theorem}
For a given elementary space $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$, maximal ideals of $M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ are of the form
$$M^p=\{f\in M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A}) : p\in\text{cl}_{\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X}Z(f) \},$$
for an unique point $p\in\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$.
head: environment

label: M^*=C(beta)
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{M^*=C(beta)}
For any measurable space $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$, the mapping $f\to f^{\beta}$ is a homeomorphism between $M^*(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ and $C(\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X)$, as Banach algebras.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\varphi :M^*(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})\to C(\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X)$ be the mapping that takes $f$ to $f^{\beta}$. By the argument preceding the proposition, $\varphi$ is one-to-one. Suppose that $\varphi(M^*(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A}))=R\subseteq C(\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X)$. Using the Stone-Weierstrass  theorem, we show that $R= C(\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X)$. First, note that, the algebra $R$ contains the constant functions. Next,  using  Corollary \ref{beta X}, for any two distinct points $p, q\in\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$ there is a measurable set $A\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}$ such that $\text{cl}_{\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X}A$ contains $p$ and not $q$. Therefore $\chi_{A}^{\beta}\in R$, $\chi_{A}^{\beta}(p)=1$ and $\chi_{A}^{\beta}(q)=0$. This shows that the algebra $R$ separates points in $\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$. 

Finally,  since  any continuous function takes closter points to closter points and $X$ is dense in $\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$, for every $f\in M^*(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$, we have $\|f\|=\|f^\beta\|$.  Therefore  $\{f_n\}\subseteq M^*(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ is a cauchy sequence in the uniform norm topology on $M^*(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ if and only if $\{f^\beta\}\subseteq R$ is so. Thus \cite[Proposition 3.1]{YEMS} implies that $R$ is uniformly closed and we are done by \cite[Theorem 44.7]{W}.
head: environment

label: beta_A N
title: Example
body_md:
\label{beta_A N}
Let $X=\mathbb N$ be the set of all positive integers and 
$$\operatorname{\mathcal A}=\{ A\subseteq X : A \text{ or } A^c \text{ is finite }\}.$$
It is clear that $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$ is an algebra in $X$ and $\operatorname{\mathcal A}^{\omega_0}=\{A\in \operatorname{\mathcal A} : A^c \text{ is finite }\}$ is an $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-ultrafilter by Lemma \ref{A-ultrafilter}(2). In fact, this is the only free $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-ultrafilter on $X$. For, if $\mathcal F$ is a distinct $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-ultrafilter on $X$, then using Lemma \ref{A-ultrafilter}(3),  there is an elementary set $A\in \mathcal F\setminus\operatorname{\mathcal A}^{\omega_0}$, i.e., $A$ is finite. Now, since $\mathcal F$ is closed under finite intersection, it is fixed. Using this, we have $\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X=\mathbb N^*=\mathbb N\cup\{\omega_0\}$, the one-point compactification of $\mathbb N$ and 
$$\bar\operatorname{\mathcal A}=\{A\subseteq\mathbb N : A \text{ is finite}\}\cup\{\{\omega_0\}\cup A : A^c \text{ is finite}\}.$$

Now, it is easy to see that $M^*(X,\operatorname{\mathcal A})$ consists only of  real-valued sequences that are finally constant, whereas $C( \mathbb N^*)$ consists of all real-valued convergent sequences.

label: beta_AX=beta X
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) $\Rightarrow$ (2). Suppose that $Z_1$ and $ Z_2$ are two disjoint zero-sets of $X$. Thus, by the assumption and \cite[Theorem 6.5(IV)]{GJ}, we have $\text{cl}_{\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X}Z_1\cap \text{cl}_{\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X}Z_2=\emptyset$. Now, since $\bar\operatorname{\mathcal A}$ is a base for open (closed) sets of $\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$, for every $p\in \text{cl}_{\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X}Z_1$, there is an elementary set $A_p\in \operatorname{\mathcal A}$ such that $p\in \text{cl}_{\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X}A$ and $\text{cl}_{\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X}A\cap \text{cl}_{\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X}Z_2=\emptyset$. Using the compactness of $\text{cl}_{\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X}Z_1$ there is a finite set of  points $p_1, ..., p_n\in\text{cl}_{\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X}Z_1$ such that 
$$\text{cl}_{\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X}Z_1\subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^n\text{cl}_{\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X}A_{p_i}\subseteq \beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X\setminus \text{cl}_{\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X}Z_2.$$
Thus $A_0=\bigcup_{i=1}^nA_{p_i}\in \operatorname{\mathcal A}$, $Z_1\subseteq A_0$ and $Z_2\subseteq A_0^c$.

(2) $\Rightarrow$ (3). Suppose that $Z_1$ and $ Z_2$ are two disjoint zero-sets of $X$. Thus, by the hypothesis, we may assume that there is $A_0\in \operatorname{\mathcal A}$ such that $Z_1\subseteq A_0$ and $Z_2\subseteq A_0^c$. It follows then, $\chi_{A_0}(Z_1)=1$ and $\chi_{A_0}(Z_2)=0$. Now, since $M^*(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ is closed in the uniform topology by \cite[Proposition 3.1]{YEMS}, the result follows from \cite[44A.1]{W}.

(3) $\Rightarrow$ (4). Using (3), we have $\operatorname{\mathcal A}=Z(X)$. Now, if $f\in C(X)$ and $U\subseteq \mathbb R$ is an open set, then $f^{-1}(U)$ is a cozero-set of $X$. Thus $f^{-1}(U)\in \{X\setminus Z : Z\in Z(X)\}=Z(X)=\operatorname{\mathcal A}$, which means that $f$ is $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-measurable, i.e., $M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})=C(X, \tau_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}})$.

(4) $\Rightarrow$ (5). It is evident.

(5) $\Rightarrow$ (1). Using the hypothesis and the argument preceding Corollary \ref{beta X}, any two disjoint zero-sets of $X$ have disjoint closures in $\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$. Now, since $\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$ is a compactification of $X$,  the result follows from    \cite[Theorem 6.5(II)]{GJ}.

label: T-compact is L-compact
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{T-compact is L-compact}
A compact elementary space $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ is $\mathcal L$-compact if and only if, the only dense open subset of $(X, \tau_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}})$ is  $X$ itself.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Just note that $\bigvee_{i\in I}A_i=X$, for a subfamily $\{A_i\}_{i\in I}$ of $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$, if and only if $\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i$ is a dense open subset of $(X, \tau_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}})$.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md: Let  $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ be an elementary space and suppose that $|X|$ is nonmeasurable. Then $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ is  $\mathcal L$-compact if and only if $X$ is finite and $\operatorname{\mathcal A}=\mathcal P(X)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ is  $\mathcal L$-compact, then it is compact as well. 
Now, using Lemma \ref{T-compact is L-compact}, $X$ is $\mathcal L$-compact if and only if $X$  is the only dense open subset of itself. But this implies that $\mathcal Q(X)=C(X)$, where $\mathcal Q(X)$ is the maximal ring of quotients of $C(X)$; see \cite[Theorem 2.6]{FGL}. Now, by the argument in \cite[3.5]{FGL},  it follows from the last equality that $(X, \tau_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}})$ is a discrete space. Hence by the compactness, we conclude that $X$ is finite  and $\operatorname{\mathcal A}=\mathcal P(X)$. The convers is evident.

label: real ideal
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{real ideal}
Let $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ be an elementary space. A maximal ideal $M$ of $M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ is called real provided that $M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})/M\simeq\mathbb R$, otherwise  is called hyper-real. Also, an $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-ultrafilter $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$ is called real whenever its corresponding maximal ideal in $M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ is real.

label: m-realcompact
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{m-realcompact}
An elementary space $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ is called realcompact  if every real maximal ideal of $M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ is fixed.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Let $(\mathbb R^n, \mathfrak M)$, for some $n\in\mathbb N$, be the Euclidean space  $\mathbb R^n$ regarded with the $\sigma$-algebra of all Lebesgue measurable sets. Moreover, let $M$ be a real maximal ideal in $M(\mathbb R^n, \mathfrak M)$. Fix some index $1\le i\le n$, and define $f: \mathbb R^n\to \mathbb R$ by $f(x_1,..., x_n)=x_i$. It is easy to see that $f\in M(\mathbb R^n, \mathfrak M)$. Now, since $M$ is real maximal, there is a real number $p_i\in\mathbb R$ such that $M(f)=M(p_i)$. This implies that $Z(f-p_i)\in Z[M]$, but 
$$Z(f-p_i)=\underbrace{\mathbb R\times ...\times\mathbb R\times \{p_i\}\times\mathbb R\times ...\mathbb R}_\text{ n factors}.$$
It follows then  $\{p\}=\{(p_1,..., p_n)\}=\bigcap_{i=1}^{n}Z(f-p_i)\in Z[M]$ which means that  $M$ is fixed and hence $(\mathbb R^n, \mathfrak M)$  is realcompact.

label: Theorem 8.4
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{Theorem 8.4}
Let $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ be an elementary space and $p\in\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$. Then $M^p$ is a real maximal ideal  if and only if $ f^*(p)\ne\infty$, for every $f\in M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The necessity is due to Lemma \ref{value of f*}(1). To prove the sufficiency, suppose that the condition hold and define $\phi : M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})\to \mathbb R$ by $\phi(f)=f^*(p)$. Then, this is a well-defined ring epimorphism, where $\text{ker}(\phi)=M^p$. Thus $M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})/M^p\simeq\mathbb R$ and $M^p$ is real.
head: environment

label: real ideals
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{real ideals}
 Let $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ be an elementary space and $M^p$ ($p\in\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$) be a maximal ideal of $ M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$. Then $M^p$ is real if and only if $Z[M^p]$ has the countable intersection property.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Sufficiency. Suppose, on the contrary, that $M^p$ is not a real maximal ideal, i.e., $p\notin\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$. Thus, by Corollary \ref{Theorem 8.4}, there is a $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-measurable function $f\in M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ such that $f^*(p)=\infty$. It follows then, $A_n=\{x\in X : |f(x)|\ge n\}\in Z[M^p]$ and clearly $\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty A_n=\emptyset$, a contradiction.

Necessity. Suppose, on the contrary, that  there is a countable subfamily $\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ of $Z[M^p]$, such that $\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty A_n=\emptyset$. Without loss of generality, we may assume that $A_{n+1}\subseteq A_n$, for any $n\in\mathbb N$. This implies that for any infinite subsequent $I$ of $\mathbb N$, we have $\bigcap_{n\in I} A_n=\emptyset$. Now, it is easy to see that the family
$$\operatorname{\mathcal A}'=\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\cup \{A^c_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\cup\{X, \emptyset\},$$
is a $\sigma$-algebra in $X$ and $\operatorname{\mathcal A}'\subseteq \operatorname{\mathcal A}$. Thus, the argument preceding the theorem implies that $\bar i(p)\in\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}'}X$ (i.e., $M^{\bar i(p)}$ is real),  where $\bar i$ is the elementary extension of $i : (X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})\to (X, \operatorname{\mathcal A}')$. In addition, using the same argument, we have $M^{\bar i(p)}=M^p\cap M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A}')$ which implies that $\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\subseteq Z[M^{\bar i(p)}]$. This, contradicts the fact that $M^{\bar i(p)}$ is real maximal, as $\bigcap_{n\in I} A_n=\emptyset$, see \cite[Theorem 3.9]{ABS}.

label: Extension into realcompact
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Extension into realcompact}
Let $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ be an elementary space and $\varphi$ be an $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-measurable mapping  from $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ into a  realcompact topological space $Y$. Then $\varphi$ extends to  a continuous mapping $ \varphi^\circ: \upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X\to Y$. Moreover, if  $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$ is a $\sigma$-algebra and $Y$ is second countable, then the extended mapping $\varphi^\circ$  is $\bar\operatorname{\mathcal A}_R$-measurable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The hypothesis implies that $ \varphi: X\to Y\subseteq \beta Y$ is $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-measurable and thus it extends to a continuous mapping $\bar\varphi :\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X\to \beta Y$, by Theorem \ref{Extension into compact}. Let $\varphi^\circ=\bar\varphi|_{\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X}$. Now, if $p\in\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$ then $\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p=Z[M^p]$ has the countable intersection property, by Theorem \ref{real ideals}. Thus, $\varphi^{\#}\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$ (see the proof of Theorem \ref{Extension into compact}) has the countable intersection property as well. It follows from this and \cite[Lemma 8.12]{GJ}, that $\varphi^{\#}\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$ is fixed and hence $\bar\varphi(p)\in Y$, i.e., $\varphi^\circ(p) :\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X\to Y$ is well-defined.

To prove the last part, first  note that  $ \bar\operatorname{\mathcal A}_{R}$ is a $\sigma$-algebra in $\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$, whenever $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ is a measurable space, by \cite[Theorem 2.4]{AABS}. Next, since $Y$ is completely regular, the family  $\mathcal B$ consisting of zero-sets with non-empty interior constitute a base for the open sets, by \cite[3.2(b)]{GJ}. Now, using second countability of $Y$, there is a countable subfamily $\mathcal B_0$ of $\mathcal B$ which is a base for the open sets, by \cite[Theorem 1.1.15]{E}. Thus, if $U$ is an open subset of $Y$, for any point $p\in U$, there exists a zero-set-neighborhood $Z_p\in\mathcal B_0$ of $p$ which is contained in $U$. This implies that 
$$U=\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}Z_n=\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}\text{int}_Y Z_n,$$
for some countable subfamily $\{Z_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ of $\mathcal B_0$. The rest of the proof is similar to the proof of Theorem \ref{Extension into compact}.
head: environment

label: uX properties
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{uX properties}
Every elementary space $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$, has a realcompact extension $\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$ which is contained in $\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$ and has the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$ is the largest subspace of $\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$ in which every $f\in M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ has a continuous extension $f^{\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}}\in  C(\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X)$. Moreover, if $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$ is a $\sigma$-algebra, then $f^{\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}}\in M(\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X, \bar\operatorname{\mathcal A}_R)\subseteq C(\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X, \tau_{\bar\operatorname{\mathcal A}_R})$.
\item $(\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X, \bar\operatorname{\mathcal A}_R)$ is the smallest realcompact  extension of $X$.
\item If $X\subseteq T\subseteq\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$ and $\operatorname{\mathcal A}'=\bar \operatorname{\mathcal A}|_T$, then $\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}'}T=\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$.
\item If $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$ is a $\sigma$-algebra, $X\subseteq T\subseteq \upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$ and $\{A_n\}_{n\in\mathbb N}\subseteq\operatorname{\mathcal A}$, then
$$\text{cl}_T\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n=\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}\text{cl}_T A_n.$$
\item Every $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-measurable mapping  from $X$ into any realcompact topological space $Y$, extends continuously to   $\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$. 
\item Every  elementary homomorphism $\varphi$ from $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ into any realcompact elementary space $(Y, \tilde A)$,  extends to an elementary homomorphism on $(\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X, \tau_{\bar\operatorname{\mathcal A}_R})$. 
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, we prove that $(\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X, \bar\operatorname{\mathcal A}_R)$ is realcompact. To do this, let $\mathcal F$ be a real $\bar\operatorname{\mathcal A}_R$-ultrafilter on $\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X $ and define $\mathcal F_0=\{A\cap X : A\in\mathcal F\}$. Since for any $A\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}$, we have $\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X\setminus\text{cl}_{\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X}A=\text{cl}_{\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X}(X\setminus A)$, it is easy to see that $\mathcal F_0$ is an $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-ultrafilter on $X$; see also Lemmas \ref{m-sets of extensions} and \ref{A-ultrafilter}(2). On the other hand, by Theorem \ref{real ideals},  if $\{A_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\subseteq \mathcal F$ then there is $p\in\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty A_n\subseteq\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$. This implies that $\{A_n\cap X\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$, where $\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$ is the unique real $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-ultrafilter on $X$, obtained by Corollary \ref{Extensions}, that is convergent to $p\in\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$. Another application of Theorem \ref{real ideals} shows that, $\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty A_n\cap X\ne\emptyset$, i.e., $\mathcal F_0$ is real. This means that $\mathcal F_0$ is convergent to a point $p_0\in\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$. Therefore $p_0\in\bigcap_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}\in\mathcal F}A$ and $\mathcal F$ is fixed,  as $\text{cl}_{\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X}(A\cap X)=A$, for any $A\in\bar\operatorname{\mathcal A}_R$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item This is due to Corollary \ref{Theorem 8.4}. The last part, is a special case of Proposition \ref{Extension into realcompact}, as  $\mathbb R$ is second countable.
\item  Let $(T, \operatorname{\mathcal A}')$ be a realcompact elementary    extension of $X$  and  $p\in \upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$. Moreover, let $\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$ be the unique real $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-ultrafilter on $X$, obtained by Corollary \ref{Extensions}, that  converges to $p$ and define $\operatorname{\mathcal A}^{'p}:=\{ A'\in \operatorname{\mathcal A}' :  A'\cap X\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p \}$. A straightforward argument, using Lemmas \ref{m-sets of extensions} and \ref{A-ultrafilter}(2), shows that $\operatorname{\mathcal A}^{'p}$ is an $\operatorname{\mathcal A}'$-ultrafilter on $T$. On the other hand, since $\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$ has the countable intersection property, by Theorem \ref{real ideals},  if $\{A'_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq \operatorname{\mathcal A}^{'p}$, then 
$$\emptyset\ne\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty (A'_n\cap X)=\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty A'_n\cap X,$$
which implies that $\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty A'_n\ne\emptyset$, i.e., $\operatorname{\mathcal A}^{'p}$ is real by the same theorem. Now, as $T$ is realcompact,  $\operatorname{\mathcal A}^{'p}$ is fixed and it is easy to see that $ \operatorname{\mathcal A}^{'p}$ is convergent (in $\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X=\beta_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}'}T$) to $p$ and thus $p\in T$, i.e., $\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X\subseteq T$.

\item Since $T\subseteq\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$ and the latter  is  realcompact by the first argument, $\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}'}T\subseteq \upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$, by part (2). On the other hand, since $\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}'}T$ is a realcompact extension of $X$, $\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X\subseteq \upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}'}T$, by part (2).
\item  Let $p\in \bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}\text{cl}_T A_n$ and $\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$ be the unique real $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-ultrafilter on $X$, obtained by Corollary \ref{Extensions}, convergent to $p$. 
Using the same corollary,     $A_n\in \operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$. Now, since   $\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$ is closed under countable intersection, by \cite[Theorem 3.9]{ABS}, we conclude that $\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$. This means that $p\in \text{cl}_T\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n$, by Corollary \ref{Extensions}. As the reverse inclusion is evident, we are done.
\item This is duo to Proposition \ref{Extension into realcompact}.
\item This is done, by applying the same proof of Theorem \ref{m-homo extension}. Only note that, $\varphi^{\#}\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$ has the countable intersection property, whenever $\operatorname{\mathcal A}^p$ is so, see Theorem \ref{real ideals}.
\end{enumerate}

label: real measurable is realcompact
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{real measurable is realcompact}
If an elementary space $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$  is realcompact, then $(X, \tau_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}})$ is a realcompact topological space.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Using \cite[Lemma 8.12]{GJ} a topological space $X$ is realcompact if and only if every prime $z$-filter which is closed under countable intersection is fixed. Note that $M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})\subseteq C(X, \tau_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}})$, which implies that $\operatorname{\mathcal A}\subseteq Z(X)$. Now, suppose that $\mathcal F$ is a prime $z$-filter on $X$ which has the countable intersection property and let $\mathcal F_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}=\mathcal F\cap \operatorname{\mathcal A}$. Since $\operatorname{\mathcal A}\subseteq Z(X)$, it is clear that  $\mathcal F_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}$ is a  $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-ultrafilter, by Lemma \ref{A-ultrafilter}(2), and it has the countable intersection property.  Thus, Theorem \ref{real ideals} implies that $\mathcal F_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}$ is a real $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-ultrafilter on $X$ and hence it is fixed. We assume that $p\in\bigcap\mathcal F_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}$ and show that $p\in\bigcap\mathcal F$. Suppose, on the contrary, that $p\notin Z$, for some $Z\in\mathcal F$. Since $Z\subseteq X$ is closed and $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$ is a base for the open (closed) subsets of $(X, \tau_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}})$, there exists some $A\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}$ such that $p\in A\subseteq X\setminus Z$. Then $Z\subseteq X\setminus A$ and therefore $X\setminus A\in\mathcal F$, as $X\setminus A\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}\subseteq Z(X)$. But, this implies that $X\setminus A\in\mathcal F_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}$ and $p\notin X\setminus A$,  which is  a contradiction. This  shows that $\mathcal F$ is fixed and hence $(X, \tau_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}})$ is realcompact by \cite[Lemma 8.12]{GJ}.

label: realcompact&realmeasurable
title: Example
body_md:
\label{realcompact&realmeasurable}
Let $\omega_1$ be the first uncountable ordinal and $X=\mathbb W=\{\alpha : \alpha<\omega_1 \}$ be the set of all countable ordinals.  For any ordinal number $\alpha$, the set of all ordinals less than $\alpha$ is denoted by $W(\alpha)$, in particular $\mathbb W=W(\omega_1)$. For any ordinal number $\alpha$, $\mathbb W\setminus W(\alpha)$ is called a tail in $\mathbb W$; see \cite[5.12]{GJ}, for more details on the space of (countable) ordinals.  Now, let 
$$\operatorname{\mathcal A}=\{ A\subseteq X : |A|\le\aleph_0 \text{ or } |A^c|\le\aleph_0\},$$
where  $\aleph_0$ is the least infinite cardinal number. It is easy to see that $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$ is a $\sigma$-algebra in $X$. Obviously, $\tau_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}$ is the discrete topology on $X$ and since $|X|=\mathfrak c$ is a nonmeasurable cardinal, $(X, \tau_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}})$ is a realcompact topological space by the argument after \cite[Corollary 8.18]{GJ}. However
$$\operatorname{\mathcal A}^{\omega_1}=\{A\in\operatorname{\mathcal A} : A \text{ contains a tail in } \mathbb W\},$$
is a free real $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-ultrafilter in $X$. In fact, if $A_0\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}$ and  $A_0\notin\operatorname{\mathcal A}^{\omega_1}$, then $A^c$ contains a cofinal subset of $\mathbb W$ and since no countable set in $\mathbb W$ is cofinal by \cite[5.12(a)]{GJ}, we conclude that $A_0^c$ is uncountable. This shows that $A_0^c\in \operatorname{\mathcal A}^{\omega_1}$; otherwise, a similar argument implies that $A_0$  is uncountable, which contradicts the definition of measurable sets of $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$. Moreover, another application of \cite[5.12(a)]{GJ} implies that  $\operatorname{\mathcal A}^{\omega_1}$ is closed under countable intersection.  Hence $\operatorname{\mathcal A}^{\omega_1}$ is a real $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-ultrafilter by Lemma \ref{A-ultrafilter}(2) and \cite[Theorem 3.9]{ABS}, which is clearly free.

As a matter of fact, this is the only free real $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-ultrafilter in $X$ and $\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X=\mathbb W^*=W(\omega_1+1)$ and
$$\bar\operatorname{\mathcal A}_R=\{A\subseteq X : |A|\le\aleph_0 \}\cup\{A\cup\{\omega_1\} :      A\subseteq X \text{ and } |A^c|\le\aleph_0\}.$$ 
 Indeed, if $\operatorname{\mathcal A}^q$ is a distinct  real $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$-ultrafilter in $\mathbb W$, then there are disjoint measurable sets $A$ and $B$ of $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$ such that $A\in \operatorname{\mathcal A}^{\omega_1}$ and $B\in \operatorname{\mathcal A}^q$, by Lemma \ref{A-ultrafilter}(3). This implies that $B\subseteq W(\alpha)$, for some $\alpha<\omega_1$, and hence $W(\alpha)\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}^q$. Now, since $W(\alpha)=\bigcup_{\sigma<\alpha}\{\sigma\}$ and $\operatorname{\mathcal A}^q$  is closed under countable intersection by \cite[Theorem 3.9]{ABS}, there exists $\sigma<\alpha$ such that $\{\sigma\}\in\operatorname{\mathcal A}^q$, i.e., $\operatorname{\mathcal A}^q$ is fixed.

title: Question
body_md: Under what conditions on an algebra $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$, do we have $ \upsilon X=\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$?
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $\mathcal B$ be a nonempty family  of subsets of a set $X$.  Then  $<\mathcal B>=\bigcup_{\alpha<\omega_1}\mathcal B^\alpha$, where $\mathcal B^0=\mathcal B \cup \mathcal B^c$ and  for any countable ordinal number $\beta>0$, 
$$\mathcal B^\beta=\{\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B^{\alpha_n}_n : B^{\alpha_n}_n\in \mathcal B^{\alpha_n} \text{, } \alpha_n<\beta\}\cup \{\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty B^{\alpha_n}_n : B^{\alpha_n}_n\in \mathcal B^{\alpha_n} \text{, } \alpha_n<\beta\},$$
where $\omega_1$ is the first uncountable ordinal number and $\mathcal B^c=\{B^c : B\in\mathcal B\}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Using \cite[5.12(a)]{GJ}, every countable family of countable ordinal numbers has a supremum less than $\omega_1$ and thus
 $\bigcup_{\alpha<\omega_1}\mathcal B^\alpha$ is closed under countable union. Now, it is enough to show that it is closed under complement operation, as in this case clearly $\bigcup_{\alpha<\omega_1}\mathcal B^\alpha$ is the smallest $\sigma$-algebra which contains $\mathcal B$ and then we are through. We prove this by the principle of transfinite induction. Clearly, for any $B\in \mathcal B^0$, we have $B^c\in \mathcal B^0\subseteq \mathcal B^1$. Now, suppose that for every ordinal number $\alpha<\beta$, if $B\in \mathcal B^\alpha$ then $B^c\in \mathcal B^{\alpha+1}$. Let $B=\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B^{\alpha_n}_n\in \mathcal B^\beta$, where $B^{\alpha_n}_n\in\mathcal B^\alpha_n$ and $\alpha_n<\beta$. Thus by the inductive assumption, $X\setminus B^{\alpha_n}_n\in \mathcal B^{\alpha+1}$ and therefore $B^c=\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty X\setminus B^{\alpha_n}_n\in\mathcal B^{\alpha_0}\subseteq \mathcal B^{\beta+1}$, where $\alpha_0=sup\{\alpha_n : n\in\mathbb N\}\le\beta$. Similarly, if $B=\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty B^{\alpha_n}_n\in\mathcal B^\beta$, then $B^c\in\mathcal B^{\beta+1}$ and thus we are done.

title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Let $\mathcal F$ be a real $\operatorname{\mathcal A}_z$-ultrafilter on $X$ and define 
$$ \mathcal F_z:=\{Z\in Z(X) : Z\in\mathcal F \}=\mathcal F\cap Z(X).$$
First, since $Z(X)\subseteq \operatorname{\mathcal A}_z$ and zero-sets are closed under countable intersection, it is easy to see that $\mathcal F_z$ is a prime  $z$-filter on $X$ which is closed under countable intersection and thus it is fixed, by \cite[Lemma 8.12]{GJ}.

 Next, we show that $\mathcal F_z$ is a $z$-ultrafilter. To this end, suppose that  $Z_0=Z(f)\in Z(X)$ and $Z_0\cap Z\ne\emptyset$, for every $Z\in\mathcal F_z$. We claim that $Z_n=f^{-1}[\frac{-1}{n}, \frac{1}{n}]\in \mathcal F_z$, for every $n\in\mathbb N$. If it is not the case, then $C=X\setminus f^{-1}[\frac{-1}{m}, \frac{1}{m}]\in  \mathcal F$, for some $m\in\mathbb N$; see Lemma \ref{A-ultrafilter}(2). It follows that, the zero-set $D=X\setminus f^{-1}(\frac{-1}{m+1}, \frac{1}{m+1})$ belongs to  $\mathcal F$ and hence to $\mathcal F_z$, as $C\subseteq D$. But $Z_0\cap D=\emptyset$, which is a contradiction. This proves the claim, and since $\mathcal F_z$ is closed under countable intersection, then $Z_0=\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty Z_n\in \mathcal F_z$. Therefore, $\mathcal F_z$ is a $z$-ultrafilter, by the argument after \cite[Theorem 2.6]{GJ}. Now, as $\mathcal F_z$ is a fixed $z$-ultrafilter, if   $x\in\bigcap\mathcal F_z$ then a zero-set $Z$, belongs to $\mathcal F_z$ if and only if $x\in Z$.

 Finally, we show that $x$ belongs to any member of $\mathcal F$, which means that $\mathcal F$ is fixed and then we are through. Using the preceding lemma, $\operatorname{\mathcal A}_z=\bigcup_{\alpha<\omega_1}\mathcal B^\alpha$, thus we prove the last statement by the principle of transfinite induction, as $\mathcal F=\bigcup_{\alpha<\omega_1}\mathcal F\cap\mathcal B^\alpha$. To show that $x$ belongs to every member of $\mathcal F\cap \mathcal B^0$, clearly it is enough to prove that it  belongs to every cozero-set of $X$, in $\mathcal F$. To let this end, suppose that  $D=X\setminus Z\in\mathcal F$, for some zero-set $Z\in Z(X)$. This implies that $Z\notin\mathcal F_z$ and since $\mathcal F_z$ is a $z$-ultrafilter, we conclude that $x\notin Z$, i.e., $x\in D$.


 Now, suppose that $x$ belongs to every member of $\mathcal F\cap \mathcal B^\alpha$, for any ordinal number $\alpha<\beta$. If $B=\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B^{\alpha_n}_n\in\mathcal F\cap\mathcal B^\beta$, then $B^{\alpha_m}_m\in\mathcal F$, for some $m\in\mathbb N$, as $\mathcal F$ is closed under countable intersection, by \cite[Theorem 3.9]{ABS}. Thus $x\in B^{\alpha_m}_m\subseteq B$, by the inductive assumption. On the other hand, if $B=\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty B^{\alpha_n}_n\in\mathcal B^\beta$, then $B^{\alpha_n}_n\in\mathcal F$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$, as $\mathcal F$ is an $\operatorname{\mathcal A}_z$-filter. Hence $x\in \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty B^{\alpha_n}_n=B$, by the inductive assumption and we are done.
\item  Let $\mathcal F$ be a real $\mathscr B$-ultrafilter on $X$ and define $ \mathcal F_z=\mathcal F\cap Z(X)$. 
Since every zero-set is a Borel set,  a similar argument as in part (1), shows that $\mathcal F_z$ is a fixed real $z$-ultrafilter. Thus, if $x\in \bigcap\mathcal F_z$, a zero-set $Z\in Z(X)$ belongs to $\mathcal F_z$ (and hence to $\mathcal F$) if and only if $x\in Z$. Now, using this fact and complete regularity of $X$ which turns the zero-sets of $X$ into a base for the closed sets of $X$ (by \cite[Theorem 3.2]{GJ}) we conclude that $x$ belongs to every closed  member  of $\mathcal F$. On the other hand, if $U$ is an open subset of $X$, then by the assumptions  $U=\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty F_n$   is an $F_\sigma$-set, i.e., a countable union of closed sets. Therefore, by the fact that $\mathcal F$ is closed under countable intersection, if $U\in\mathcal F$ then there is some $m\in\mathbb N$ such that $F_m\in\mathcal F$ and hence $x\in F_m\subseteq U$. This implies that  $x$ belongs to every member of $ \mathcal F\cap \mathcal B^0$, where $\mathcal B^0=\tau\cup\tau^c$; see the preceding lemma. The rest of the proof is similar to the argument of part (1). 
\end{enumerate}

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Hom}
If $D$ is a dense ideal of $M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$, then $\text{Hom\,}D\subseteq C_L(\text{coz\,}D)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\varphi\in\text{Hom\,}D$. If $x\in\text{coz\,}D=:V$, choose an elementary function $d\in D\subseteq M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ such that $d(x)\ne0$ and define
$$g(x)=\frac{\varphi(d)(x)}{d(x)}.$$
Whenever $d'\in D$ is another elementary function for which $d'(x)\ne0$, since $\varphi$ is a $M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$-module homomorphism, then $d'\varphi(d)=d\varphi(d')$. This shows that, $g$ is a well-defined real-valued function on $\text{coz\,}D$. To prove that $g\in C_L(V)$, let $p\in V$ and suppose that $g(p)=\frac{\varphi(d)(p)}{d(p)}=r_0$, for some suitable $d\in D$. Moreover let, $A_0=\text{coz\,}d$, $A_1=d^{-1}(r_1)$ and $A_2=\varphi(d)^{-1}(r_0r_1)$, where $r_1=d(p)\ne0$. Since both  $d$ and $\varphi(d)$  belong to $M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$, we conclude that $A_0, A_1$ and $ A_2$ are elementary sets, see the argument before Lemma \ref{units}. Hence, $p\in A_0\cap A_1\cap A_2\subseteq V$ and $g(x)=\frac{\varphi(d)(x)}{d(x)}=r_0$, for any $x\in A_0\cap A_1\cap A_2$.
Now, if $d\in  D$, for any $x\in V$ and a suitable choice of $d'\in D$ we have
$$\varphi(d)(x)=\frac{\varphi(d')(x)}{d'(x)}d(x)=g(x). d(x),$$
which means $\varphi(d)=g.d$. This  shows that $\varphi=g\in C_L(V)$.

label: Q(M(X))
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{Q(M(X))}
Let $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ be an elementary space, then
$$\mathcal Q(M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A}))=\lim_{\substack{\longrightarrow \\ V\in\mathcal V_0(X)}}C_L(V),$$
where $\mathcal V_0(X)$ is the family of all dense open subsets of $X$.

title: Corollary

\label{Max quotient of M}
If $(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ is a measurable space, then $\mathcal Q(M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A}))=\mathcal Q(X)$.

title: Corollary
body_md: If an algebra $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$ in a set $X$ contains all  one-point subsets  of $X$, then $\mathcal Q((M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A}))=\mathbb R^X$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Using the hypothesis $\{ \{x\} : x\in X\}\subseteq \operatorname{\mathcal A}$, which implies that $\tau_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}=\mathcal P(X)$. Thus, by  Corollary \ref{Q(M(X))}, we conclude that
$$\mathcal Q(M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A}))=\lim_{\substack{\longrightarrow \\ V\in\mathcal V_0(X)}}C_L(V)= C_L(X)=\mathbb R^X,$$
as the only dense open set in the discrete space $(X, \tau_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}})$, is $X$ itself.

title: Remark
body_md: Note that, by \cite[1.2]{FGL}, the classical ring of quotients of a ring $R$ (denoted by $\mathcal Q_{\text{cl}}(R)$) is the ring  of equivalence classes of  formal quotients $r/s$, where $r\in R$ and $s$ is a non-zero-divisor of $R$. If $R$ is a regular (von-Neumann regular) ring,    since    all its non-zero-divisors are unit, we have $\mathcal Q_\text{cl}(R)=R$. Now,  Lemma \ref{multiple elements} implies  that  $M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$ is regular and  thus we conclude that $\mathcal Q_\text{cl}(M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A}))=M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})$.

title: Example
body_md:
Let $X=\mathbb W$ be the set of all countable ordinals and $\operatorname{\mathcal A}$ be the $\sigma$-algebra described in Example \ref{realcompact&realmeasurable}. As it pointed out in that example, $(X, \tau_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}})$ is a discrete space and hence $Z(X)=\mathcal P(X)$. Now, it is easy to see that $|Z(X)|\ne |\operatorname{\mathcal A}|$, thus $Z(X)\ncong\operatorname{\mathcal A}$ and therefore $M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})\ncong C(X, \tau_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}})$, by Proposition \ref{M=C(X)}.

On the other hand, using Example \ref{realcompact&realmeasurable}, $\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X= \mathbb W^*=W(\omega_1+1)$ and
$$\bar\operatorname{\mathcal A}_R=\{A\subseteq X : |A|\le\aleph_0 \}\cup\{A\cup\{\omega_1\} : A \text{ contains a tail in }\mathbb W \}.$$
Therefore, $\tau_{\bar\operatorname{\mathcal A}_R}=\mathcal P(X)\cup \{A\cup\{\omega_1\} : A \text{ contains a tail in }\mathbb W \}$. Using Lemma \ref{Z(X)=B(X)} and the argument after Definition \ref{real ideal}, $Z(\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X)=CO(\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X)$, the set of all clopen subsets of $\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$. Now, let $B\in CO(\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X)$ be a clopen subset of $\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X$. If $\omega_1\in B$, then $B\cap X$ contains a tail in $\mathbb W$ as $B$ is open; otherwise, since $B$ is closed, $B\subseteq X$ and $|B|\le\aleph_0$. This shows that $Z(\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X)=\bar\operatorname{\mathcal A}_R$ and hence $M(X, \operatorname{\mathcal A})\simeq C(\upsilon_{\operatorname{\mathcal A}}X)$, by Proposition \ref{M=C(uX)}.
